paragraphs.heading: What a polar climate is
paragraphs.text: A polar climate is one with no warm summer, though its winters can differ from place to place. Every month averages below 10 °C. In the Köppen climate classification it is marked with the letter E. Summers are cool and winters very cold, or there is no real summer at all, which leaves treeless tundra, glaciers or a lasting layer of ice. Together these regions cover more than 20% of Earth's area.

paragraphs.heading: Tundra and ice cap
paragraphs.text: There are two types. Tundra, coded ET, has at least one month averaging above 0 °C, while ice cap, coded EF, has none. In tundra not even conifers can grow, but specialised plants such as the arctic poppy can. In an ice cap climate no plants grow at all, and ice slowly builds up until it flows or slides somewhere else.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are
paragraphs.text: Most polar regions lie near the poles, where winter days are very short and summer days very long, sometimes for a whole season or more. Antarctica is the only continent where the ice cap type dominates, and nearly all of Greenland has it too, apart from coastal strips that have tundra. Tundra covers the far north of Eurasia, much of northern Siberia, northern Iceland, and large parts of northern Canada and Alaska. Many high mountain summits are polar as well; when the cold comes from height rather than latitude, it is called an alpine climate.

paragraphs.heading: Why the Arctic is milder
paragraphs.text: The Arctic is an ocean almost ringed by land such as Russia and Canada. Its seawater can never drop below −2 °C, so it softens the climate around it. In winter this comparatively warm water, even under the ice pack, stops the North Pole from being the coldest spot in the Northern Hemisphere, and it helps explain why Antarctica is so much colder. Antarctica has the coldest climate on Earth, with −89.2 °C measured at Vostok Station in 1983. It is also so dry that it counts as a polar desert, averaging 166 mm of precipitation a year, since weather fronts seldom reach far inland.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the line with trees
paragraphs.text: Climatologist Wladimir Köppen linked the Arctic and Antarctic tree lines to a summer temperature of 10 °C: where the warmest month averages below that, forests cannot grow. Otto Nordenskjöld argued that winter matters too, with the formula W = 9 − 0.1 C, where W is the warmest month's average and C the coldest month's, both in °C. So a place whose coldest month averages −20 °C needs a warmest month of at least 11 °C for trees to survive, since 9 − 0.1(−20) = 11.
